text.p: Go-Ahead Group has set its sights on longer-term overseas growth through rail and bus deals and is currently "prospecting" for a deal in Poland and other central European countries, the transport group said in an interview.

Go-Ahead, which was confirmed as winner of the lucrative Thameslink rail franchise in the UK on Tuesday, failed in its bid for Swebus of Sweden which was eventually clinched by rival Stagecoach. But commercial director Chris Moyes told Reuters that overseas expansion remained a top priority and plenty of other opportunities remained.

"We have a presence in Poland and are exploring possible partnerships with others. It could be in buses or rail. The potential of Poland or central Europe is the first likely step overseas -- but it could take a long time to come to fruition," he said.
"The moves in Poland at the moment mean that we hope we will be involved if they franchise out their transport links."

Moyes added that UK transport companies were well placed to expand on the continent because of their role in the deregulation and sell-off of the UK bus market and privatisation of rail which is now close to completion.
"We've been through it in the UK already -- so British companies are ideally poised to exploit these opportunities."
"Our achievement in London has been good. A company that has 1,000 buses in London has a fair degress of credibility in these overseas markets," Moyes said.

Expanding onto the continent is seen as a necessary next step for players like Go-Ahead, which has no businesses outside the UK at present. The UK rail franchise sell-off is now almost complete and the bus market offers little potential for expansion. The two factors have proved to be major drivers of share price growth for the entire sector in recent years.
Moyes said there were now a number of dynamics behind the changes in continental Europe.
The first is the financial straitjacket imposed on those countries seeking to enter the European single currency in the first wave in 1999.
"We see Maastricht convergence as a factor, as most of Western Europe, and possibly central Europe, will need to find ways of reducing the subsidy of public transport systems.
"We are therefore seeing moves towards deregulation and privatisation all over Europe. Rail franchising was at first seen as a joke. Now Europe sees it's not such a daft idea."
"A lot of European companies threw cash at their transport systems for years. They cannot afford it anymore."
Moyes said the European Commission-inspired move to separate transport infrastructure from operators also created the ideal framework for privatisation.
"Germany and France are both moving to separate infrastructure from operators. The Netherlands is fairly well advanced in looking at segregation," he said.
On Go-Ahead's plans for the Thameslink rail franchise, Moyes said there was huge potential to develop the line as a fast-link to Gatwick airport from London's financial district.
Go-Ahead won the franchise with French partner VIA-GTI , owning 65 percent and 35 percent of the GOVIA bid, respectively.

The GOVIA team was confirmed as the winner of Thameslink earlier Tuesday and will receive a 2.5 million stg subsidy in year one of its franchise, paying a premium of 28.4 million to the government by 2004.
The line's passenger revenue in the year ended March 31 1996 was 76 million.
